strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting language-model pretraining losses early enough to inform training decisions. Modeling loss by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective.

The experimental coverage is substantial, spanning dense models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, ID and OOD evaluation, and additional fitting experiments with GPT-NeoX and MoE architectures. The position-dependent loss curves show consistent empirical regularities.

Section 2.4 evaluates prediction of subsequent checkpoints from early training observations, providing stronger evidence than retrospective curve fitting alone. The reported improvements over power-law, reciprocal, and logarithmic baselines across three larger model sizes are promising.

The data-mixture application connects forecasting to completed training outcomes. The selected mixtures improve ID and OOD perplexity over both proxy-model selection and selection using observed 10B-token losses, with improvements in 12 of 14 downstream task/model comparisons.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor incorporates the known cosine schedule and training horizon, whereas the baselines lack this structure. After a0 and a1 are frozen, Equation 10 reduces to a constant plus a2(N). A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same piecewise log-log/cosine structure and schedule information is therefore an essential control. Its absence leaves the claimed source of improvement unresolved.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture and package tables. The outlier-filtering threshold, nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, and actual evaluation interval are unspecified. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, applies calibration when Npred <= Nsep, contradicting the post-separation calibration described in Section 2.4. Appendix H also omits the exact mixture candidates and search size. These consequential ambiguities, together with the missing comparison above, prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The generic-law claim exceeds the tested scope. Training uses the Pile, the LLaMA tokenizer, and cosine learning-rate schedules. OOD evaluation does not establish robustness to different training corpora or schedules. The GPT-NeoX and MoE extensions primarily demonstrate retrospective fits rather than early-checkpoint forecasting. The claims should explicitly reflect these boundaries.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence needs stronger uncertainty and ranking analysis. ID perplexity improves from 8.65 to 8.58 and from 7.55 to 7.50, but independent-run variability or confidence intervals are not reported; averaging five neighboring checkpoints does not establish run-to-run reliability. Selection occurs after 10B tokens, whereas the main forecasting evaluation begins at 40B. Reporting candidate predictions, final outcomes, and forecasting errors at the actual selection cutoff would substantiate this application.

The theoretical arguments are weaker than claimed. Appendix C rejects exponential decay after arbitrarily setting its additive offset to zero; a positive offset removes that objection. Equation 17 follows from imposing constant a0 and a1, and equal observed loss-decrease rates do not establish that position reweighting cannot help. The three suppression experiments support a limited empirical observation about the tested strategies.

The novelty framing needs correction. Kaplan et al. (2020), already cited, also investigates learning curves as a function of training steps, so describing temporal loss modeling as unexplored is too broad. The contribution should be positioned around the particular token-position decomposition and forecasting procedure, with a focused comparison to existing learning-curve models.
